The EU's AI transparency rules (Article 50 of the AI Act) started applying on 2 August 2026. They reach any provider or deployer serving EU users, so a US or UK freelancer with EU clients is not automatically outside them.

Most of the panic is overblown. Three things actually matter for a one-person business: a chatbot on your site has to tell people it's a chatbot, realistic AI-made images/audio/video of real people or events have to be disclosed, and AI text published to inform the public on matters of public interest has to be labelled. Your service page written with ChatGPT's help is not a press release about public affairs.

The slides have the exact lines you can paste under a bot greeting and under AI visuals. Twenty minutes, once, and it's done. Reported penalties run to €15 million or 3% of worldwide turnover, which is why "I'll deal with it later" is a bad plan — and why this is a workflow, not legal advice. If you work in health, finance or law, pay a lawyer for an hour.

Save this so it's there next time you ship an AI-made asset. If you've already added a disclosure line, post the wording you used — other people can steal it.

"Did you use AI on this?" is now a normal client question. The EU's AI transparency rules started applying on 2 August 2026 and procurement teams have noticed. You want your answer written down before someone asks it in an email at 9pm.

One paragraph in your proposal does it. Where AI helps, where it never touches, who is accountable. The last part is the one clients care about: you are. Nobody is asking you to work by hand. They're asking whether their data went somewhere and whether a human checked the output.

The prompt on slide 3 drafts the paragraph from your own boundaries. Rewrite it in your words afterwards — a clause that sounds like a chatbot wrote it defeats the point.

Month-end bookkeeping is the job that eats a Sunday. The part that changed: QuickBooks can now pull transactions out of a PDF or image of a bank statement, and its categorisation suggestions come with an explanation of why it guessed that. Xero and FreshBooks are pushing the same reconciliation and invoicing automation.

That kills the typing. It does not kill the checking. The workflow on the slides is: let the software extract and categorise, then spend your attention on the twenty transactions that actually matter — biggest amounts, anything uncategorised, anything it explained badly.

Then export the CSV and use the prompt on slide 3 in ChatGPT or Claude to find the things software doesn't flag: the subscription you're paying twice, the client whose invoices got slower every month. Strip names and account numbers first. Your bank data is not chatbot training material.

Save this before the end of the month. What's the one expense you always forget to log?

The tools stopped being chatboxes this summer. OpenAI launched ChatGPT Work on 9 July 2026 and a small business program on 21 July. Anthropic started rolling Claude Cowork out to web and mobile on 7 July, Max subscribers first. All of them run multi-step jobs instead of answering one message.

Which changes the skill. Chatting gets you a paragraph. A brief gets you a finished thing. The template on slide 2 is the same one you'd hand a subcontractor: the artefact, what "done" means, the inputs it may use, the constraints, and permission to ask instead of guess.

The line that saves you most is the last one — ask for a list of what it skipped. Agents fail quietly. They'll hand you a confident deliverable with two invented figures in it and no flag. If you can't verify the output in five minutes, don't delegate that job yet.

Save this for the next job you'd rather not do yourself. What's the first task you'd hand over?

"Can you just add a couple of slides?" Four hours later you've done it for free and the client has no idea they asked for anything.

Scope creep isn't a boundaries problem, it's a paperwork problem. Nobody writes the change order because writing it feels aggressive and takes twenty minutes you don't have. So you eat it. The fix is to make the email cost two minutes and sound normal.

Log the request the day it lands — date, what they asked, your estimate. Then run the prompt on slide 3. It gives you a short, warm, unapologetic email that names the extra hours, the price, the new date, and offers a swap for something already in scope. The swap is what makes it land: you're not refusing, you're pricing.

One thing AI won't do: hold the line. It writes the email. You still have to send it before you do the work, not after.

Save this for the next "quick favour". How many unpaid hours did the last one cost you?

OpenAI launched a ChatGPT for small business program on 21 July 2026 — training, guides, agents aimed at owners who are the marketer, the accountant and the salesperson at once. Useful. But none of it fixes the actual problem: the model doesn't know your rates, your clients, or the work you refuse.

So write one page. Services and prices, who you serve, who you turn down, three words for your tone, and one rule about never inventing numbers. Slide 3 has the skeleton — it takes fifteen minutes.

Then stop retyping it. Paste it into a ChatGPT Project or Claude Project so every chat in that folder starts with it, or drop it into Custom Instructions. Every draft comes back closer to something you'd actually send.

It won't make outputs true. Context makes them sound like you, which is exactly when a wrong price is hardest to spot — so still read the numbers.

An invoice is 31 days late and you've sent nothing, because every draft you start sounds either apologetic or furious. So it sits there, and your bank balance sits with it.

Stop writing one email. Write the whole ladder in one go: day 1 after due date (friendly, assume oversight), day 14 (firm, restate the terms and the late fee, ask for a payment date), day 30 (final notice, work pauses, name the next step). The prompt on slide 3 drafts all three in about a minute. Save them, schedule them, stop rewriting them for every client.

The uncomfortable part: emails don't collect money, terms do. If your contract has no payment window and no late fee, no wording gets you paid faster — you're asking a favour. Fix the contract for the next client while you chase this one.

Anthropic announced on 10 August 2026 that new Claude models embed an invisible watermark in the text they generate, plus signed provenance metadata (C2PA) on files. It applies worldwide, not only in the EU, and the mark is designed to survive copy-paste.

Before you panic about the draft you sent last week: the mark shows Claude processed a piece of text, not that Claude wrote it. Paraphrasing breaks the signal, and the public detection tool has not shipped yet. Nobody is scanning your proposal today.

The workflow that actually protects you is the same one that makes the work better: rewrite the draft from your own notes so the facts, numbers and judgement are yours, and put one honest line about AI use in your terms so it never becomes a mid-project argument. Not legal advice — read your own contracts.

Every solo business has the same leak: proposals that were sent, never answered, and never chased. Not because you don't care — because Monday starts and the work in front of you wins.

Claude Cowork can run a task on a schedule — daily, weekly or monthly — against a folder of your own files, and hand back a working spreadsheet. So point it at your proposals folder and let it do the remembering. You get a table with the stale ones flagged and a draft follow-up for each.

Honest limitation: it misreads amounts on scanned PDFs and it will mark a closed deal as open. Treat the output as a to-do list, not a source of truth. Two minutes of eyeballing, three emails sent, done before your coffee goes cold.

The habit is worth keeping even though the tab is gone. Ten minutes of research before a first call is the difference between "so, tell me about your business" and a question that makes them sit up.

The prompt below forces citations and an UNVERIFIED label, because the failure mode here is confident nonsense: wrong headcount, invented funding round, a director who left two years ago. If you automate work in Notion, the billing changed under you. Since May 2026, Notion's custom agents run on metered credits: pooled across the workspace, reset monthly, no rollover. Full Notion AI sits on the paid Business tier.

Metered means an agent that loops spends money while you sleep. So the question stopped being "can I automate this?" and became "is this job worth paying per run?"

Here is the test I use: it has to repeat at least weekly, touch five or more records, and be something you skip when you get busy. One out of three, do it by hand or paste a prompt into a normal chat — that is included and it is fine. The prompt below writes a tight spec with a stop condition, which is the difference between a useful agent and a meter running in the dark.

The cheapest sales asset you own is the job you just finished. Written up as a one-page case study, it does the arguing for you in the next proposal — and most solo operators have zero of them.

Write the copy first, design second. The prompt below gives you the structure: short headline, three bullets, one client quote, one line on what you'd do next. No adjectives, numbers where you have them.

Then let Canva do the layout. Canva AI 2.0 (April 2026) keeps a memory of your style and reapplies it, so the second one-pager looks like the first without you fiddling with fonts. Canva Sheets plus bulk create will produce one per row if you have a few jobs to write up.

Two honest limits: AI layout will happily stretch your logo and invent a statistic, so check every number against your own invoice — and never publish a client name or logo without asking first.

The invisible cost of finishing a project is the six months of "quick questions" afterwards. Where's the file, how do I change the header, who do I call when it breaks. All unbilled.

Fix it once with a handover pack. Put your delivery files into a NotebookLM notebook — final deliverable, SOW, decisions log, a checklist of accounts (names only, never passwords) — then generate the client-facing doc from those sources only. NotebookLM answers from what you upload, which is exactly what you want here: no invented steps.

Add a Video Overview from the same notebook. NotebookLM turns notebook content into a narrated video summary, and a five-minute walkthrough kills most of the follow-up calls.

Honest limit: it treats every uploaded file as true, including the superseded draft you forgot to remove. Delete old versions first, then read the whole thing before it goes out with your name on it.

The most valuable five minutes of your week is straight after a client call, when you still remember the budget number they mumbled. Two days later it's gone, and your follow-up email is vague.

OpenAI's release notes say GPT-Live in ChatGPT Voice now supports file uploads and Projects as of 7 August 2026. So keep one Project per client, and talk into it while the call is fresh: on the walk back, in the car park, before the next thing starts.

Talk for two minutes, then let it produce the follow-up email, a line on what they agreed versus what they asked for free, and the open questions. The scope line is the one that saves you money later.

Honest limit: voice transcription drops digits and mangles surnames. Fix names and numbers by hand before anything with a price on it leaves your outbox.

You paste a client's numbers into the same chat you used for someone else's pitch. Nothing bad happens. Then a proposal comes back with the wrong industry in it.

Fix is boring. One ChatGPT project per paying client. Files, chats and instructions live in it, and the memory setting stays project-only so context doesn't wander between accounts. That setting used to be locked at creation — you can now change it in Project settings after the fact.

The standing brief on slide 4 is the part that saves the time. Scope, out of scope, who you're writing for, how they talk. Write it once when you sign, never re-brief again.

One honest caveat: project-only memory is organisation, not confidentiality. If the contract says no third-party processing, that clause still wins.

You've uploaded the same client brief eleven times. Once per chat, because the last chat got too long.

As of mid-August 2026, ChatGPT can see your Google Drive properly: browse files and folders from the Library, or pull a file into any chat from the composer or with an @mention, without uploading it again. Files shared with you show up too.

So the workflow changes shape. One Drive folder per client — contract, brief, brand notes, last three deliverables. Then the weekly update prompt on slide 4 points at two files and gives you shipped / blocked / next week, with the contract quoted for scope.

Limitation worth respecting: it reads what you point it at, it doesn't verify it. An old brief in that folder gets quoted as gospel. Clean the folder before you trust the output.

Your pipeline lives in one sheet. Forty rows, twelve columns, and you stopped opening it in March.

Google started rolling out Gemini in the Sheets side panel in August 2026, including canvases: click Create canvas, describe the view you want in plain English, and refine it with more prompts until it's right. No formulas, no pivot tables.

The view that actually pays you is on slide 4. Group by stage, sort by due date, highlight anything that's delivered and unpaid, highlight anything with no next action. That's your Friday twenty minutes.

Honest limits: creating and editing canvases has per-user usage limits, you need Workspace smart features on, and the rollout is staged — if the Gemini icon isn't there, you're waiting. It also can't rescue a tracker you don't keep current.

The part people miss about Claude's text watermark: it isn't only for text Claude wrote.

Anthropic's own explainer says the mark indicates text was processed by Claude. Paste in a paragraph you wrote yourself for a proofread, a translation or a summary, and the output carries the mark. It travels with copy-paste and can persist through some editing. The EU has required providers serving its market to mark AI-generated content since 2 August 2026, and other major model developers signed the same code, so this won't stay a Claude-only thing.

Two things that make it less alarming. Anthropic says the watermark carries no identifying information and can't be traced back to a person, organisation or chat, and nothing hidden is inserted into your text.

So the move isn't to hide it. It's slide 4: a four-line AI-use note in the proposal, before delivery. A client who already knows how you work doesn't run detectors.

Not legal advice — and absence of a mark proves nothing either way.

Save this before your next handover. Has a client asked you the AI question yet?

Your proposal prompt used to land. Now the output is flabbier and you can't say why.

Nothing changed on your side. The model did. OpenAI removed the GPT-5.1 models from ChatGPT in March 2026 and moved existing conversations onto newer ones; GPT-4.5 and o3 were each retired after a published sunset period. Prompts you tuned against an older model don't get a migration notice.

So keep the five prompts that make you money in one plain text file — proposal, follow-up, scope change, invoice chase, case study — with one good output saved next to each. That saved output is the benchmark. Without it you're arguing with your memory.

Then run slide 4 whenever your default model shifts. It compares old output to new, names what drifted, and rewrites the prompt to get the old quality back.

What it can't do: bring back a retired model. Sometimes the honest answer is that the prompt needs rebuilding.

Save this. Which of your five prompts would you notice breaking first?

A good lead in an industry you've never worked in. You've got two days and no idea what they call things.

Most people ask AI for a briefing, skim it, and walk into the call sounding like they skimmed a briefing. ChatGPT's newer quiz mode is better for this: ask it to quiz you on a topic and you answer inside the conversation, one question at a time. It's on all consumer plans, web and mobile.

Slide 3 is the prompt. Fifteen questions on how they make money, what goes wrong in the job, who signs off, and the vocabulary. Graded and corrected as you go. Then five questions to ask them and three claims to avoid.

The gaps it exposes are the real output. Ask the client those things directly — clients like being asked how their business works.

One limitation: the quiz is generated, not sourced. Anything you'll repeat as fact in the meeting, check against a real source first.

Save this before your next discovery call. What's the sector you keep bluffing?

You've been pasting client material into ChatGPT for a year without reading the confidentiality clause. Most people have.

Ten minutes fixes it. Slide 3 makes the model quote every clause that limits sharing with third parties or sending data abroad, then give you a flat yes / no / unclear per clause, then draft the email that asks the client. Quotes matter — you want the wording, not a reassuring summary.

If the answer is no, redacting and working on structure only usually gets you most of the value. Asking permission gets the rest; clients often say yes once you name the tool. Running a model on your own machine is a genuine third option now — Meta released Muse Glimmer in August 2026 under an Apache 2.0 licence, a 30B model that runs on a Mac or PC with one decent GPU — but it's slower and weaker than what you're used to, so treat it as the last resort, not the default.

This is not legal advice. A model misses cross-references and local law. For a regulated client, pay a lawyer once and reuse the answer forever.

The catch: the free tier still maxes out immediately. Pro is worth the $20/month if you're building anything that takes more than a few turns.

NotebookLM just added full notebook copying. That means research notebooks with all your sources, artifacts, and chats now copy as a complete unit—not piecemeal.

Useful when you're handing off research to a client, archiving a project, or building a template for work you do repeatedly.

The limit: sources follow your Google AI plan limits, so check your tier. Comment what you use NotebookLM for—research, client work, or learning.

ChatGPT's Google Drive integration just matured: you can now browse your Drive directly from the Library, pull files into chats without uploading again, and keep Docs/Sheets/Slides open side by side while you work.

The catch: ChatGPT reads what you point it at. If you drop a stale brief or old pricing list, it will quote it confidently.

Save this if you're pulling documents into ChatGPT constantly. Comment: do you hand it confidential files?

Invoicer.ai is built from the ground up around natural language: you describe line items and rates in plain English and it drafts a complete invoice instantly.

Faster and cleaner than legacy form-based tools. Good fit if you want AI-assisted invoicing without the weight of a full accounting suite.

The catch: invoice-only. No balance sheet, no KPI dashboard, no accounting breadth. You're not outsourcing bookkeeping—you're just drafting invoices faster.

Save if you send a lot of invoices. Comment: what's your current bottleneck—drafting or chasing payment?

Claude Opus 4.6 shipped in February with a 1 million token context window (beta) and 128K max output tokens—roughly double prior limits. Same price as Opus 4.5.

Means you can drop multiple long research papers, full client briefs, or years of email into one chat and ask it to synthesize across all of them without splitting into multiple conversations.

The catch: beta means it can be slow and the 1M window is not available in all configurations yet. The 200K window is the practical default.

Save this if you work with large documents. Comment: what's the longest document you've ever dropped into Claude?

Perplexity's Deep Research searches dozens of sources across hundreds of pages, compiles citations, flags contradictions, and generates a structured report—all in 2–5 minutes.

Use it for competitive analysis, market sizing, technical research, or anything where you need a cited briefing, not just a hot take.

The catch: Deep Research is on Pro (paid) only. It's also a research tool, not a decision-maker—contradictions flagged still require human judgment.

Save this if you do a lot of research for proposals or client work. Comment: what would you research first?

OpenAI is retiring the official DALL·E GPT on August 30, 2026. If you're using it to generate images, you need to switch to ChatGPT Images before then.

ChatGPT Images does the same work—create and edit images—without a separate tool. Simpler and one less login.

User-created GPTs with image generation enabled are not affected. Only the official one is going away.

Save this if you use DALL·E through ChatGPT. Comment: are you using DALL·E, or did you already switch to ChatGPT Images?
